title: Reverse Engineering ME2's USB with a Heat Gun and a Knife
originalTitle: Reverse Engineering ME2's USB with a Heat Gun and a Knife
content:
Reverse Engineering ME2's USB with a Heat Gun and a Knife

Background

In 2024, bjiru uploaded a video about the ME2 handheld device, a toy produced around 2008 that featured the ability to use USB to synchronize points and gems between your device and an online world. The game was extremely niche, so no software, drivers, or assets had been archived, at least until bjiru came forward with the online game client.

I am the leader of Miuchiz Reborn, an effort that started in 2015 to preserve, reverse engineer, emulate, and maintain the accessibility of a game similar to this one, with an online portion and a handheld portion connected via USB. Due to the similar vintage and type of game, the ME2 had already been brought to my attention by my Miuchiz community in 2018, since they thought (mistakenly) that they might share architectural similarities. Despite me being aware of the device's existence for years, bjiru's video finally prompted me to begin research on it.

My initial efforts were spent solely on recreating the server required to make bjiru's copy of the computer game functional again, but along the way, my attention inevitably drifted to the handheld. A recreation of the online game surely could never be complete without the mechanism to synchronize your points to and from the device. This communication between your computer and the ME2 device was the game's main gimmick, after all. I figured that my prior experience with the Miuchiz handheld devices would help me make short work of untangling whatever communication ritual they expect... as long as I could get some code to reverse engineer.

My curiosity demanded the sacrifice of ME2s. EBay demanded the sacrifice of fiat money. Before long, these specimens lay before me.

These are small units with only a couple of buttons and a female mini-USB port. There's a cable included in the box, but it's lacking any disk for software and drivers. That USB port would be the way to synchronize points between your computer and the handheld, but when I embarked on the same journey for the Miuchiz handheld device, I attained full access to its flash memory by reverse engineering how its accompanying Windows software worked. With no such software for the ME2, there is nothing to reverse engineer to figure out how to communicate with the device. Even after checking the Wayback Machine and bjiru, there were apparently no surviving copies of whatever software used to talk to these things. I think it was called ME2 Desktop Buddy, but that application was separate from the game client that bjiru recovered. The handheld does expose itself as a removable storage device, but the contents just direct you online to download the ME2 game, which is no longer available.

The way forward is clear, since there's only one option left: open the hardware.

What's inside

The main ME2 firmware is stored on an SST39VF3201, a 2 megaword (4 megabytes, with 16-bit addressable units) flash chip. The main microcontroller is... under a hard epoxy glob-top. This is known as a chip-on-board (CoB) and is usually a cost-saving measure, but it has the side effect of hiding any identifying information about the integrated circuit inside. A regularly packaged chip will usually have markings that identify it, just like the flash chip does. Since microcontrollers used in devices like these often contain an internal ROM, it's possible that parts or all of the USB code that I wanted to reverse engineer were in that ROM. Having that code in ROM has the benefit of allowing recovery of a bricked device or, if the manufacturer chooses to do so, flashing the device after assembly. That ROM would exist inside a chip which I had no way of identifying.

Retrieving the data from the flash chip is a straightforward and well-documented process: desolder the chip, put it into an off-the-shelf flash programmer like those by XGecu, and use it to dump the contents. If I need information off the microcontroller's ROM as well, then that is less straightforward, but it's still doable for a device like this where protection is unlikely. In the past, I added code to the SPI flash on a Tamagotchi Pix that would copy its boot ROM to free space on the flash chip, which could then be read by the same flash programmer that I used to inject the code. However, in that case, the microcontroller was properly packaged and had model information printed on it, so I could find its datasheet to know what instruction set it used and where its ROM was in the memory space. At this point, I had none of that information for the ME2's mysterious chip-on-board.

Extraction

Despite uncertainties, the only apparent way forward from here is to desolder the flash chip. I had also purchased some sockets for the flash chip in hopes that I'd be able to solder one to the handheld's PCB. This would allow me to reprogram the ME2 and quickly iterate if I needed to write code for it to dump the internal ROM from the microcontroller.

Unfortunately, I was unable to get the flash chip off with a soldering iron without damaging the chip. To resolve this skill issue after multiple failed attempts, I instead purchased a rework station (effectively a heat gun that claims to be able to reach 500 °C) and removed the chip by melting the solder with hot air. This allowed me to dump the contents of the flash with no issue, but it revealed that actually using the sockets I had purchased was going to be beyond my capabilities. Not only would I have to solder all 48 tiny pins onto the PCB, I would also have to do it quickly enough to avoid melting the plastic on the sockets. I had neither the tools nor the skill to deal with that, so if I needed the ROM, I'd need another strategy.

The dump looked good, though, and using a tool I had already built specifically for finding uncompressed bitmaps in firmware dumps, I could find images that would ordinarily be displayed on the device:

Instruction Set Discovery

I've obtained a dump of the firmware from the flash chip, but before serious reverse engineering can be done, I at least need to know what instruction set the device runs. There were no markings on the hardware itself, so it'd have to be guessed. I tried analyzing the code in Ghidra, an open source disassembler, decompiler, and janky nightmare that keeps me employed, with just about every type of processor spec it came with. Any ARM variant? Some 6502 descendant? MIPS? Literally anything else supported by Ghidra? All a resounding "no."

I tried everything, and nothing would disassemble this code. I knew it was code, because I could even find parts of the code I was looking for!

Because of my past work on the Miuchiz handheld device, I had some familiarity with how USB mass storage devices worked. I identified this snippet to be almost certainly moving 'U', 'S', 'B', 'S' somewhere, which is a signature specifically for the kind of USB mass storage communication that I was looking for. Some or all of the USB code that I needed to reverse engineer to figure out how to interact with this device was definitely in this flash dump, but with no clue as to what instruction set it was written in, I couldn't disassemble it.

At this point, I had a couple of broken ME2 units. It seems stupid, but perhaps there are markings somewhere under the epoxy blobs? Probably not, but for the research phase, sometimes a completely decimated unit is more valuable than one that is simply broken.

Well, I had a heat gun, and I had a knife. As they say, when you have a heat gun and a knife, everything looks like... a nail? I think that's how the saying goes.

Setting the rework station to its maximum temperature and prying with a knife liberated the entire epoxy blob. Its departure revealed no markings underneath the chip-on-board-now-off-board. You can see the underside of the microcontroller's silicon die, though, and the epoxy has a couple of air bubbles through which you can see bond wires.

As I said, sometimes a decimated unit is worth more than a broken unit, and I had a heat gun, a knife, and a dire need to brush up on my idioms.

Oh.

Huh.

I had no idea you could decapsulate a CoB that way. It just popped out cleanly, and given its temperature, I'm glad it didn't do that in my direction. It's very pretty, but there is actually a way forward from here. Let me just get a closer look with my electron microscope.

Well, that's what its user manual claims it to be. To be fair, I checked, and it does contain at least one electron.

While destroying "hacking" other toys whose small components challenged my eyes, it became obvious that I rarely knew what was going on at the other end of my soldering iron. A very courteous recommendation from a friend resulted in the purchase of a cheap digital microscope, intended for coins and soldering.

Despite it not really being suitable equipment for the job, counter to its user manual's claims, I captured this image with the microscope. It is leagues away from being able to decipher any text on the die, but the general layout is clear, and I knew where I could find more images like this one.

Siliconpr0n, now known as Siliconprawn, has an archive where many people have uploaded die shots, albeit usually in better quality than mine. Unfortunately, there is no useful way to search the site given the information I had, so I started clicking, and scrolling, and repeating...

Its fingerprints are on the record!

After several hours, at 4 AM, I finally spotted something familiar. It's better quality than mine, but the layout is unmistakable. I have a GPL162002A (or B) rotated 180 degrees when compared to the matching image taken by John McMaster. It's a GeneralPlus microcontroller, its datasheet is available on the internet, and its instruction set is μ'nSP.

Reverse Engineering the Firmware

μ'nSP, as it turns out, is fairly common for toys of this type and vintage. Hopefully, I can be forgiven for not guessing it was an instruction set whose name contains characters that aren't even in the Latin alphabet. Despite that, it's still niche enough to not be supported by Ghidra out of the box. Fortunately, there is some existing third-party work for it, so I was able to start disassembling it in Ghidra, naming functions, and importing register names from the datasheet.

Here's the function that I was so certain was USB code just from its hex dump, interacting with USB registers as specified in the microcontroller's datasheet:

As I previously noted, I was already somewhat familiar with how USB mass storage devices like this communicate, especially due to some experimental work porting my Miuchiz USB library to macOS using libusb. USB mass storage devices essentially tunnel SCSI commands, and those are well documented online. For example, there are commands to request a read from or a write to the device.

However, I knew that in general, the standard commands, like for read or write, wouldn't be useful to me. Those are what your computer already knows how to do with its built-in mass storage drivers. It will issue those to interact with it like any ordinary removable media device. In this case, the read command will just retrieve the filesystem containing the help file, and the write command will do nothing, since it is not supposed to be writable. These are not for interfacing with the entire flash chip; instead, they are effectively a tiny simulated CD-ROM to help first-time users.

Some command IDs, however, are reserved for whatever the vendor wants to implement. Handlers for some reserved IDs are crudely injected before the normal ID lookup runs.

Through static analysis, I was able to identify and name the functions that I was looking for: read, program, and erase flash. These are all nonstandard commands that were implemented for the ME2 and possibly other GeneralPlus devices, and almost certainly used by whatever software and drivers originally came with the device. You can craft a USB message to trigger any of these paths. Read lets you retrieve data from flash. Program lets you "program" flash. Erase lets you reset all bits in a flash region to 1, which when used in combination with the program command, can issue a full write to flash, since "programming" can only flip bits from 1 to 0. Each one of the custom commands I was interested in uses the reserved ID 0xFF followed by IDs for sub-commands and any parameters the operation needs.

The exact structures of the commands are not particularly relevant for the reader, but the methodology might be. I used libusb (well, actually, rusb) to facilitate all of my interaction over USB. This method allows you to write userland code to interact with your USB device, as opposed to writing a new driver.

When the Windows ME2 software disappeared from the internet, it was as if the second-to-last speaker of its language died. The ME2 handheld device became, in a sense, a terminal speaker. With a little bit of experimentation and a little bit of reading sometimes-correct decompilation, I was reading its mind to learn the words of its nearly extinct language. When it spoke back, I knew I was on the right track.

Č̶̯a̴̩͗n̵͉͆ ̴͍͠Ǐ̶̜ ̴͈͌h̷̙̔á̶͉v̸͈̽é̴̢ ̵͍͛a̵̞͝ ̴̤̉s̵̡͊ē̴̮c̸̭̅t̶̛͖o̸̡͠r̶̺̊ ̶̥̀ǫ̸̀f̸̦́ ̷̈́ͅỳ̷͎o̶̦̐u̵͙̚r̶͙͒ ̵̥̕f̸̡͝l̷͈̄a̶͍͋s̸̢̓h̸̗͝?̴̪̕

...No? Must be my accent. Let me adjust and ask again: Can I have a sector of your flash? What about the next sector? Are you willing to program any of the bits in that sector? Can I have your flash again to see if it's different now? Dare I ask you to erase a sector... and hopefully understand which one I'm asking you to destroy?

One by one, I wrote the code to structure, populate, and transmit the messages I needed the ME2 to hear. Once we were on the same page, I told it to send me a couple of flash dumps while having different amounts of points. After comparing them, I was able to identify where points are stored in flash and finally use my computer to modify them!

Indeed, I could do whatever I wanted to the device using these commands, as long as it didn't involve erasing code that was actively being used. The ME2 joined my collection of devices that display the Miuchiz Reborn emblem in places it shouldn't be, including the digital microscope that took the die shot.

"Embadded" ROM and "Embadded" Bugs

Admittedly, the first time I tried to read/write flash, I was being a bit reckless, because I couldn't see all the code that was executing. For instance, some code calls into the microcontroller's internal ROM, or into RAM routines copied there by the ROM. Some of my guesses for the other functions were informed by how direct memory access (DMA) registers got set up. If DMA is set up to copy from the USB buffer, for example, it's probably using that data to program the flash, not to read from the flash.

This code, for example, calls a function residing outside of flash, so that it doesn't pull code out from under itself, before returning to the code that it just pulled out from under itself anyway. You do have to be very careful to not brick the device.

The memory region in question is clearly laid out by the datasheet:

There are 128 kilowords of particularly "embadded" ROM that I didn't yet have access to, preventing me from fully understanding the system.

Fortunately, the function for the custom flash read command doesn't perform bounds checking. This means that with a specially crafted message that attempts a read from a very high flash address, you can wrap around the microcontroller's entire address space, ending up back at the start. Because this amounts to an arbitrary read capability, I didn't need to write any on-device dumping code this time! All of memory is readable with this bug, so I used it to read the Embadded ROM, which I saved for later reverse engineering.

With all of memory, I was able to spot the device's framebuffer in RAM, displaying the image that was on the device's screen at the time:

I was also able to read the general purpose I/O (GPIO) registers from the device's address space by referencing where the datasheet said they should be. By triggering the bug dozens of times per second, I could effectively poll for button presses and turn it into a USB controller if I wanted: (Video)

At some point during my testing, I noticed a strange modification of a value in flash which didn't even seem like it was supposed to be save data.

0x00AA (remember, this system's word size is 16 bits) has been written to a place in flash that I didn't ask for. With the Embadded ROM, we can finally see the code that explains this.

These flash chips take commands by writing to specific offsets. Unlike RAM, which immediately commits written data, the flash chip will only try to interpret writes as part of a command, so a single write to the flash's address space is not sufficient to actually change any data. When a piece of code wants to program flash, it issues a multi-step command sequence that starts by writing 0xAA to 0x5555 and ends by writing the desired data at the desired address.

If a user with too much spare time (and perhaps a heat gun and a knife) comes up with the idea to try probing for how the device works, they may end up requesting the device to program to a sector that is beyond the capacity of its flash chip. The processor is aware of every step, but the flash chip is not. Instead, that final command cycle misses the flash chip's address space entirely, so the flash eagerly awaits what value should be programmed where.

Processor: Hey flash! I want to start programming another word!

Flash: Loud and clear! Programming 0xAA to 0x5555!

Processor: ...Huh?

Due to the desynchronized command cycles, the flash confuses the first cycle of the next command for the last cycle of the previous command, and 0xAA gets programmed to 0x5555. The equivalent address for typical 8-bit bytes is 0xAAAA, which matches where 0x00AA got written to in my flash dump.

This could potentially be used for an arbitrary write, as long as you are okay with corrupting that specific word in flash, but the device is already sufficiently pwned that I'm not interested in bricking more units. It might be possible to save these devices, as reverse engineering the Embadded ROM also showed that it contains its own USB handler and flash read/program/erase implementations. However, I have only ever gotten the ROM to enter that state (instead of booting into flash code) once, and never again. Based on the ROM's decompilation, I suspect it might rely on a GPIO port that has been left floating, but I'm not sure. In any case, my mission here had already been accomplished.

Final Products and Takeaways

The end result of this mischief is a command-line utility that can:

  • Read flash
  • Write flash
  • Read points
  • Set points
  • Read gems
  • Set gems
  • Dump memory (via exploit)
  • Watch button input (via exploit)

This, along with game server code and other research, is available in the ME2-Restoration repository. Since implementation details are available there and are likely not interesting to the typical reader, specific technical details were omitted here in favor of describing processes and techniques.

More importantly, this demonstrates that the original PC-side software is not strictly required to understand or preserve its functionality. Even with the official software lost to time, it was possible to open up the black box that was the ME2 and reconstruct its protocol from its hardware and firmware, restoring an otherwise dead interface into something usable again. This is not limited to interfaces like USB, either. Read how I recreated a long-dead license server to bring a decade-old vector editor back to life.

This is also my first time decapsulating an integrated circuit, so to pay it the respect it deserves, I purchased a better microscope and have since contributed the highest-quality photo of the GPL162002A/B to siliconprawn, previewed here at a reduced resolution for web-friendliness:
